newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan nuclear body may be broken up after accident.
newsitem.headline: Japan nuclear body may be broken up after accident.

text.p: Japan is considering breaking up the operator of a nuclear reprocessing plant which was the site last month of the nation's worst nuclear accident, a leading Japanese financial daily said on Saturday.

Most of the state-owned Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corporation (PNC) would be privatised under the break-up plan being drawn up by the Science and Technology Agency, the Nihon Keizai Shimbun said.

An explosion on March 11 at the PNC's fuel reprocessing plant at Tokaimura, 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo, exposed 37 workers to small doses of radiation and provoked a savage public reaction as details emerged of a bungled emergency operation, delays in informing the authorities and deliberate inaccuracies in an official accident report.

The newspaper quoted Science and Technology Agency officials as saying the PNC could be carved up into as many as four parts. Most of the operations would be privatised, leaving only the company's core fast-breeder reactor research programme in the public domain.
The newspaper report did not say when a final decision would be made on the plan and when it might go into effect.
Officials from the Science and Technology Agency were not available to comment on the Nihon Keizai report.

"The nuclear-fuel recycling programme will remain in place. Although the nucleus of the executive staff will remain, the dissolution and reduction of the organisation is unavoidable," the newspaper quoted a Science and Technology Agency official as saying.

Under the plan, the agency would hive off operations involving uranium enrichment and reprocessing, uranium mining, plutonium processing, and the management of high-level radioactive waste. It is not clear whether high-level waste management will be privatised, the report said.

The move comes after PNC executives admitted that they had lied in a report into the fire and subsequent explosion at the complex. In the report, submitted to the government on March 21, they said workers had visually checked to ensure the fire had been put out, but conceded last week that this was untrue.

Although officials believed the fire had been doused, it flared up again several hours later, triggering an explosion that gutted the four-storey building and released radiation into the atmosphere. The radiation leakage was classed by the government as Japan's worst nuclear accident on record.
A furious Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last week ordered a raid on PNC headquarters after PNC executives admitted the deception.
Hashimoto has said there will be a full probe by independent consultants into the accident.

Public confidence in the PNC had already been seriously shaken by a coolant leak in December 1995 at its prototype fast-breeder reactor, Monju. No one was hurt in that accident and there was no radiation leakage.
